title: Performance alert casebook and investigation scenarios
body:
Purpose and scope:

This document is a compact casebook of recent alert scenarios, investigation heuristics, and reproducible data patterns for serving-runtime performance regressions. The goal is to provide concise scenario-driven playbooks (mini-incident narratives), recommended dashboard queries, minimal repro steps for local benchmarking, and a clear bisect/canary comparison workflow that a responder can follow without needing to read the whole perf playbook.

Why a casebook?
- Most triage is pattern recognition: seeing the same metric constellation across incidents lets us triage faster.
- This file is intentionally narrative — short incident histories + distilled actions + quick checks to do first.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes)
1) Who/what: confirm service, model, and region in alert (team on-call + channel).
2) Scope: check per-route error rate and latency percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99).
3) Canary delta: compare canary vs baseline in last 1hr and 24hr windows.
4) CPU/GPU saturation: check node-level GPU Util, CPU steal, mem pressure.
5) Recent deploys: open commits in the last 6 hours (git log / CI deploys).
6) Rate change: check incoming request rate (requests/s) and avg tokens per request.
7) Rollback flag: if latency > SLO x1.5 for p99 and customer-impacting, evaluate rollback/canary rollback.

Common alert signatures and immediate hypotheses
- Pattern A: p99 latency spike with stable RPS and normal GPU util => often KV-cache misses, model cache warmup, or tokenization step regression. Quick check: prefix cache hit rate and cache eviction metrics.
- Pattern B: increased tail latency + correlation with higher variance in batch sizes => batching scheduler regression or encoder slowdown. Quick check: distribution of batch sizes and scheduling queue time.
- Pattern C: global latency increase + GPU memory creeping up across pods => memory leak or larger KV cache entries (recent patch to kvcache format). Check pod restart history and jmap/heap stats.
- Pattern D: increased 5xx errors + latency spike => upstream model runtime crashes (OOM) or new model variant incompatibility. Check kube pod statuses and model loader logs.

Mini case studies (repro steps + lessons learned)
Case 1 — "Midnight tail climb" (Nov 2024)- Symptoms: p99 latency doubled between 02:00–03:30 UTC; p50 unchanged; RPS constant.- Investigation highlights: flamegraph snapshots showed a long tail in tokenizer.normalizeText. Prometheus histogram of tokenization_duration_seconds p99 went from 3ms to 45ms.- Root cause: tokenization library upgrade introduced UTF-8 fallback path for rare characters — encountered by a small request cohort.- Quick repro: run dataset subset with non-ascii tokens and measure tokenizer timing: python tools/token-bench.py --chars nonascii --repeat 1000.- Mitigation: revert tokenizer package, add canary to push patch that disables fallback, add an alert on tokenization p95 > 10ms.- Lesson: add tokenization micro-metrics to default serving dashboards.

Case 2 — "Canary divergence after quant profile change" (Jan 2025)- Symptoms: Canary p99 increased 30% vs baseline; canary deployment used a new quantization profile.- Investigation highlights: Compare timeline graphs of kernel stalls and queue time. Canary showed more frequent GPU kernel re-launches (nvtx markers).- Root cause: quant profile triggered a fallback code path in kernel selection that used smaller kernels, increasing kernel launch overhead for short tokens.- Bisect approach: A/B the quant params in descending specificity: toggled activation clamp then weight quant step. Also re-ran the micro-benchmark harness (tools/bench_kernels.sh).- Mitigation: revert profile, engage model team to produce a tailored quant profile for llm-3-large.- Lesson: always run the kernel micro-bench matrix for representative token lengths when changing quant profiles.

Case 3 — "Traffic shift exposed batching scheduler logic bug" (Dec 2024)- Symptoms: p95 latency increased with sudden growth in variance of request size (some requests 2 tokens, some 2k tokens), batching efficiency dropped.- Investigation highlights: Scheduler logs showed increase in enqueue wait time; batch assembly algorithm had an edge-case when mixing very short and very long sequences.- Root cause: heuristic choosing max_batch based on rolling average token length failed on bimodal requests.- Quick repro: run synthetic generator: python tools/synth_load.py --mix bimodal --rps 120 --duration 600 and observe batch_size distribution.- Mitigation: patch scheduler to maintain separate short/long queues and adjust batching thresholds, then push canary and compare batch composition histograms.- Lesson: test scheduler with synthetic bimodal distributions as part of CI.

Essential dashboard and queries (prometheus / grafana)
- Latency percentiles: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) by (route, model_variant)- Batch size distribution: sum(rate(batch_assembled_count[5m])) by (size_bin, model_variant)- GPU kernel stalls: increase in nv_gpu_kernel_launchs_total{status="failed"} or custom nvtx markers- KV cache hit rate: rate(kv_cache_hits_total[5m]) / rate(kv_cache_lookups_total[5m])- Tokenization p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(tokenize_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))

Bisect/canary comparison workflow (practical steps)
1) Snapshot baseline: export metrics for baseline window (T0 = -24h to -1h). Save JSON of metrics and perf traces to artifacts S3.
2) Snapshot canary: export metrics (T1 = last 1h) and collect flamegraphs / scheduler logs.
3) Compare: generate delta histograms and visualize p50/p90/p95/p99 diffs per route/model. Tools: scripts/compare_metrics.py --baseline b.json --canary c.json --out delta.svg
4) Narrow change domain: toggle one variable at a time — kernel selection, quant profile, scheduler config. For each toggle, run short A/B canary (1% traffic or synthetic repro) and measure deltas.
5) Bisect binary: if many commits between baseline and canary, run git bisect using a short repro harness configured to run the micro-benchmark for 30s per commit: git bisect start; git bisect run ./tools/quick_bench.sh;
6) Decision gates: require p99 improvement >= 10% AND batch efficiency >= baseline OR no regressions in cache hit rates to promote rollback/merge.

Local repro and perf capture checklist
- Repro harness: tools/bench_driver.py (supports --model, --seq-len, --rps, --tokens-per-req). Use --capture-traces to get flamegraphs.- Capture flamegraphs: run under perf or py-spy: sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- ./serving_bin; perf script | ./flamegraph.pl > flame.svg- Kernel counters: use nvprof or nsight-system for GPU kernel timelines. Save .qdrep snapshots.- Scheduler logs: enable 'debug-scheduler' for the run to collect enqueue/dequeue times and batch composition.

Roles and communication template (for responders)
- Triage lead: acknowledges alert, posts incident summary and scope in #incidents.- Profiler: runs local microbench and attaches flamegraphs.- Ops: checks infra metrics and scales pods if needed.- Dev: looks for suspicious commits, opens PR to revert if confirmed.
Post in channel template:
"[INCIDENT] p99 latency spike on route: /v1/generate model: llm-3-large region: us-west-2. Initial observations: p99 up 2x, RPS stable, tokenization p95 elevated. Triage steps: collecting flamegraph and cache metrics. Assigned: @ravi (lead), @ava (profiler)."

Unresolved questions and follow-ups (for postmortem)
- Do we need a canary test harness that replays real traffic distributions (including unusual tokens)?- Should tokenization micro-metrics be enabled by default for all models? Cost vs benefit?- How to integrate kernel micro-benchmark into CI without blowing up runtime? Consider nightly matrix sampling.

Appendix: useful commands
- Export recent metrics: curl "http://prom-api/api/v1/query_range?query=request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate"}&start=...&end=...&step=60" > gen_latency.json- Run local bench: python tools/bench_driver.py --model llm-3-large --seq-len 512 --rps 50 --duration 120 --capture-traces- Run quick bisect: git bisect start HEAD v2024-11-05 -- ./tools/quick_bench.sh

Notes: keep this file small and living. Add new cases as we encounter them and link directly to archival artifacts. The mental model to carry: alerts are fingerprints — learn the fingerprint, then hunt the needle (root cause) rather than recreating the whole path each time.
